::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Limits Definition](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5153204/limits-definition), asked by [API_ DAiFUKu](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1785163/api-daifuku) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2026-10-30; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> First, this is the definition of limits I've been taught.
>
> > Let $f:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ where $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and $a$ is a limit point of $D$. $\lim_{x\rightarrow a} f(x) = L$ if and only if for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta  > 0$ s.t. if $0 < |x-a| < \delta$, then $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$, for all $x\in D$.
>
> I, as a high school student who is interested in real analysis, saw a theorem which states:
>
> > If $x\in\mathbb{R}$ s.t. $0 \le x < \varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon > 0$, then $x=0$.
>
> My question is that does the theorem implies $|f(x) - L| = 0$ or $f(x) = L$, which I think it doesn't make sense - I took $\lim_{x\rightarrow 0} \left(\dfrac{x}{x}\right)$ as an example.
:::

The difference is the order of the quantifiers and the extra variable $\delta$.

The definition of $\lim_{x\to a}f(x) = L$ means

> $\forall \epsilon > 0,\ \exists \delta > 0,\ \forall x \in D,\ (|x-a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \epsilon)$

The admissible values of $x$ depend on $\delta$, which depends on $\epsilon$.

The second theorem, in this context, reads

> $\forall x \in D,\ (\forall \epsilon > 0,\ |f(x) - L| < \epsilon \implies f(x) = L)$

In this case, $\epsilon$ is independent of $x$.
